alt: The program finds the longest strictly increasing run in a list. It keeps the current run length and the best so far, adds one when a value is larger than the one before it, and on any other step sets the run to 0 instead of 1, which is the bug the lesson tracks down.

steps.c: Python starts at the top of the file. Line 1 runs first.
Line 1 runs; line 4 is next.
Line 4 runs: the name `main` now refers to a function.
Line 19 checks the condition: it is true, so line 20 runs next.
Line 20 calls `main`. A new frame for `main` goes on top of the call stack.
`main()` starts running its body at line 5.
Line 5 runs: `raw` is created with the value `'0 0 1\n'`.
Line 6 runs: `t` is created with the value `['0', '0', '1']`.
Line 7 runs: `a` is created with the value `[0, 0, 1]`.
Line 8 runs: `best` is created with the value `1`.
Line 9 runs: `run` is created with the value `1`.
Line 10 runs: the loop gives `i` its first value, `1`.
Line 11 checks the condition: it is false, so line 14 runs next.

Line 14 runs: `run` changes from `1` to `0`. The value is not larger than the one before it, so the run ends. The code sets `run` to 0, but the new run already contains this value, so it should start at 1.
Line 15 runs; line 10 is next. `best` keeps the larger of itself and `run`, so it can only grow.
Line 10 runs: the loop gives `i` its next value, `2`.
Line 11 checks the condition: it is true, so line 12 runs next.
Line 12 runs: `run` changes from `0` to `1`.
Line 15 runs; line 10 is next.
Line 10: the loop has no values left, so it ends and line 16 runs next.
Line 16 runs: it prints `1`. The call of `main` returns `None`. Its frame leaves the call stack next.
The program has finished: no lines are left to run.
